said.text: "My vote against this bill stems primarily from the harmful impact it will have on Medicaid, affecting low-income families and rural health care providers like our hospitals and nursing homes."

src.t: Portland Press Herald

did.text: Voted NO on final passage of H.R. 1 (51-50). Her amendment to add $100 billion for rural hospitals, paid for by higher taxes on the very highest earners, failed 78-22. She had voted YES on the June 28 motion to proceed, saying a majority leader has the right to bring bills to the floor.

src.t: Senate roll call 119-1-372

statements.record: FactCheck.org (Aug 2026) rated a Democratic ad claiming she "voted to support" the Medicaid cut as false, noting her final vote against the bill while acknowledging critics' point about the procedural vote.
statements.note: Final vote matched the stated position; the procedural vote is the counterpoint critics cite.

statements.topic: Confirming Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as HHS Secretary

said.text: "In general, I give deference to presidents to build their own team." She cited Kennedy's assurances that he would not restrict access to the polio vaccine, would support Lyme-disease vaccine research, and would re-examine cuts to biomedical research funding.

src.t: Maine Public

did.text: Voted YES to confirm Kennedy (52-48).

src.t: Senate roll call 119-1-52

statements.record: A year later NPR documented that Kennedy had broken several confirmation-era commitments, including replacing the CDC's vaccine advisory committee and withdrawing vaccination-program funds.
statements.note: The vote matched her stated reasoning at the time; the commitments she relied on were later reported broken.

said.text: "I support the abortion rights established by Roe v. Wade and affirmed by Planned Parenthood v. Casey." Introduced the Reproductive Choice Act with Sen. Murkowski to codify those rulings.

src.t: Collins press release

did.text: Voted NO on cloture for the Democratic Women's Health Protection Act, saying it "goes far beyond what is necessary to codify" Roe and Casey and would override conscience protections. In 2024 she voted YES on cloture for the Right to Contraception Act.

src.t: Collins statement; roll calls 117-2-170 and 118-2-190

statements.note: Her votes track the narrower position she has stated; she opposed the broader Democratic bill on stated grounds.

said.text: "Canada is often the closest source of goods in those supply chains. Maine borders only one state, New Hampshire, but shares a 611-mile border with Canada." She has pressed the administration to review the tariffs' impact on Maine businesses.

src.t: Collins press release

did.text: Voted YES on S.J.Res. 77 (Oct. 29, 2025, passed 50-46) to end the Canada tariff emergency; one of a handful of Republicans to do so.

src.t: Senate roll call 119-1-598

statements.note: Her votes against the Canada tariff emergency match her stated concern for Maine's cross-border economy.

ethics.title: Straw-donor scheme by a defense contractor that gave to her 2020 campaign and allied super PAC
ethics.summary: Executives of Hawaii defense contractor Navatek (later PacMar Technologies) pleaded guilty to federal campaign-finance crimes for illegal contributions to Collins' 2020 campaign and $150,000 routed through a shell company to the pro-Collins super PAC 1820 PAC. CEO Martin Kao was sentenced to 87 months in prison (2025). In February 2025 the FEC fined PacMar $325,000; the Campaign Legal Center's complaint "did not allege involvement by Collins or her campaign," and the campaign disgorged the illegal contributions. In September 2026 ProPublica reported that FBI anti-corruption agents had examined Collins' relationship with Navatek and sought a broader bribery probe before the inquiry was shut down in 2025. Collins was never charged or formally accused; her office "vigorously" denies any pay-to-play and says she cooperated fully.
ethics.outcome: No finding or charge against the senator. Contractor executives convicted; FEC civil penalty against the company.

sources.t: Campaign Legal Center (FEC outcome)
ProPublica, Sept. 22, 2026
Boston Globe takeaways

did.text: Voted NOT GUILTY (57-43; 67 needed to convict). On January 6, 2021 he voted NO on sustaining the objection to Arizona's electors.

said.text: In 2018 he testified against proposed China tariffs that would hit Alaska-caught fish: "The current proposal advantages Chinese and Russian fishermen over American fishermen… I respectfully request that you change it." In 2025 his office said tariffs on Canada are leverage against fentanyl: the U.S. "should not accept any amount of deadly fentanyl coming in from either our Southern or Northern border."

src.t: SeafoodSource (2018); Alaska Beacon (2025)

did.text: Voted NO on S.J.Res. 37 (April 2, 2025) and NO on S.J.Res. 77 (Oct. 29, 2025), both of which would have ended the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian imports.

src.t: Senate roll call 119-1-598

statements.note: Opposed tariffs that hurt Alaska seafood in 2018; supported Canada tariffs in 2025 on fentanyl grounds. Different tariffs, different rationale — voters can judge the consistency.

statements.topic: Stock trading by members of Congress

said.text: The STOCK Act requires senators to disclose securities trades within 45 days. In 2022 Sullivan disclosed two inherited-stock sales about 87 days after they occurred; his office said a third-party manager had not notified him until October 30.

src.t: Anchorage Daily News

did.text: Voted YES on cloture for H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act (failed 53-47, Sept. 30, 2026), which would bar members from buying individual stocks and was paired with a voter-ID provision.

src.t: Senate roll call 119-2-253

statements.note: A documented late disclosure in 2022; supported the 2026 Republican stock-restriction vehicle.

ethics.title: Late STOCK Act disclosure of two stock sales
ethics.summary: Sales of inherited shares in Mowi ($15,001–$50,000) and Five Below ($1,001–$15,000) made in August 2022 were reported on November 3, 2022, roughly six weeks past the 45-day deadline. Sullivan's office said a third-party investment professional did not notify him until October 30 and that "the necessary steps were immediately taken." Late filings carry a $200 fee; whether it was paid was not reported.
ethics.outcome: Late disclosure acknowledged by the senator's office; no further enforcement action reported.

sources.t: Anchorage Daily News, Nov. 10, 2022
Washington Examiner, Nov. 8, 2022

statements.topic: Stock trading by members of Congress

said.text: "Members of Congress shouldn't be trading individual stocks while making decisions that move markets." Introduced the Senate Stop Insider Trading Act.

src.t: Marshall press release

did.text: Voted YES on cloture for H.R. 7008 (failed 53-47). Separately, LegiStorm reported in 2021 that stock purchases by his dependent children in early 2020 (up to $15,000 each in Chevron and Disney) were disclosed more than a year after the STOCK Act's 45-day deadline.

src.t: Senate roll call 119-2-253

statements.record: The 2021 late-disclosure report is documented in the Ethics tab.
statements.note: Current position and vote align; his own household's 2020 trades were reported late.

said.text: Responding to criticism of the bill's Medicaid changes, Marshall said "there are no Medicaid cuts." In September 2025 he said, "The goal would be to get people off Medicaid. Let's help them find a job where they get insurance."

src.t: KSN-TV; Marshall press release (Sept. 30, 2025)

did.text: Voted YES on H.R. 1 (51-50). The Congressional Budget Office estimated the enacted law reduces federal Medicaid spending by about $1.06 trillion over 2025–2034 and increases the number of uninsured by 10 million in 2034.

src.t: Senate roll call 119-1-372

statements.record: CBO cost estimate of the enacted law (July 21, 2025), as summarized by the American Hospital Association; CBO's June 2025 analysis of the Medicaid title projected 7.8 million more uninsured.
statements.note: The "no cuts" characterization conflicts with CBO's scoring of the law he voted for; his stated goal of moving people off Medicaid is consistent with the vote.

said.text: Days before taking office he announced he would object to certifying electoral votes: "We must hold accountable any state that disregarded the law or our constitution."

src.t: KSHB-TV

did.text: Voted YES to sustain the objections to Arizona's electors (rejected 6-93) and Pennsylvania's. Two days later he said, "Biden is the president-elect and there must be a peaceful transition of power on Jan. 20," and called for rioters to be prosecuted.

src.t: Senate roll call 117-1-1; Lawrence Journal-World

ethics.title: Late STOCK Act disclosure of family stock purchases
ethics.summary: LegiStorm reported that purchases by Marshall's dependent children between February 24 and July 8, 2020 — including up to $15,000 each in Chevron and Disney during the pandemic market drop — "were not included in any of his periodic transaction reports he filed as a member of the House in 2020" and surfaced only in his 2021 annual Senate report, more than a year past the 45-day deadline.
ethics.outcome: Reported as a STOCK Act reporting violation; no public penalty reported.

sources.t: LegiStorm, Sept. 30, 2021

statements.topic: Banning stock trading by members of Congress

said.text: "Members of Congress should not be playing the stock market while we make federal policy and have extraordinary access to confidential information." He pledged a ban as a 2020 candidate and placed his own portfolio in a blind trust in 2021.

src.t: Ossoff press release

did.text: Sponsored the Ban Congressional Stock Trading Act (2022, reintroduced 2023). On Sept. 30, 2026 he voted NO on cloture for the Republican-written Stop Insider Trading Act (H.R. 7008), which Senate Democrats called "toothless" because it exempted the executive branch and which carried an attached voter-ID requirement.

src.t: Senate roll call 119-2-253; CBS News summary

statements.record: CBS News: Democrats "viewed the voter ID provision as a 'poison pill' designed to force them to oppose stock-trading restrictions."
statements.note: A long record of sponsoring a ban; opposed the 2026 Republican vehicle on stated grounds of scope and the attached voter-ID language.

said.text: In a July 2020 campaign ad Ossoff pledged to refuse corporate PAC donations.

src.t: Thomasville Times-Enterprise

did.text: FEC filings for Jan. 2025–June 2026 show about $903,000 in itemized PAC receipts: roughly 54% from other Democrats' leadership PACs and campaign committees, 23% from labor unions, 7% from ideological groups, and the rest from professional and trade associations (for example, the National Beer Wholesalers Association, Mortgage Bankers Association and National Association of Broadcasters PACs). No company-sponsored corporate PAC appears in the filings reviewed.

src.t: FEC Schedule A, line 11C (filings listed in the Funding tab)

statements.note: Consistent with the pledge as commonly defined (company PACs). He does accept trade-association and leadership-PAC money, which critics count as corporate-adjacent.

statements.topic: Immigration enforcement — the Laken Riley Act

said.text: "Laken Riley was my constituent, and her family are my constituents. And she never should have been killed. It was preventable… we're going to have to be vigilant as we move forward, that we defend our borders and enforce our immigration laws."

src.t: PolitiFact (quoting a radio interview)

did.text: Voted YES on cloture (Jan. 9, 2025) and YES on passage of S. 5 (64-35). PolitiFact rated his opponent's claim that he "voted against the Laken Riley Act" False.

src.t: Senate roll call 119-1-7

statements.note: Votes match the stated position.

ethics.title: FEC civil penalty: late refunds of excessive and prohibited 2020 contributions
ethics.summary: The FEC's Reports Analysis Division referred Jon Ossoff for Senate for failing to timely remedy $363,272.43 in excessive, prohibited and impermissible contributions received during the 2020 general and runoff elections (from individuals including foreign addresses, non-qualified PACs, LLCs, unregistered organizations and a corporation). The committee was asked about the money in March 2021 but did not complete refunds until June 2023. In a negotiated settlement (ADR 1142) the committee agreed to a $27,000 civil penalty, a written compliance policy and outside compliance training, attributing the lapse to its external compliance vendor.
ethics.outcome: $27,000 civil penalty paid; remedial compliance measures required.

sources.t: FEC ADR 1142 — RAD referral 23L-54
FEC ADR 1142 — negotiated settlement

said.text: "I heard from constituents today asking about corporate PAC contributions. I'm joining several of my colleagues & no longer accepting these contributions."

src.t: CNBC

did.text: FEC filings for Jan. 2025–June 2026 show about $480,000 in itemized PAC receipts: roughly 82% from other Democrats' leadership PACs and campaign committees, 10% from labor unions and 6% from ideological groups. One trade-association PAC (American Hotel & Lodging Association, $5,000) appears; no company-sponsored corporate PAC was found.

src.t: FEC Schedule A, line 11C (filings listed in the Funding tab)

statements.note: Consistent with the pledge's terms; PAC money now comes mostly from fellow Democrats' leadership PACs and unions.

statements.topic: Importing cheaper prescription drugs from Canada

said.text: Booker said the Klobuchar–Sanders budget amendment "didn't adequately make sure foreign drugs meet American safety standards."

src.t: Roll Call

did.text: Voted NO on the amendment (rejected 46-52) on Jan. 11, 2017 — then, on Feb. 28, 2017, co-introduced a drug-importation bill with Sen. Sanders that added the safety language he had cited.

src.t: Senate roll call 115-1-20; Axios

statements.record: Critics noted Booker was among the top Senate recipients of pharmaceutical-industry contributions at the time.
statements.note: A no vote followed within weeks by co-sponsoring a version of the same policy.

statements.topic: Stock trading by members of Congress

said.text: Senate Democrats, including Booker, opposed advancing the Republican Stop Insider Trading Act, calling it "toothless" for exempting the executive branch and objecting to an attached voter-ID requirement.

src.t: CBS News via AOL

did.text: Voted NO on cloture for H.R. 7008 (failed 53-47).

src.t: Senate roll call 119-2-253

statements.note: Vote recorded with the caucus's stated reasons; no individual Booker statement on the vote was located.

statements.topic: Money in politics and single-issue PACs

said.text: "The problem is money and politics. And I think I want to lead by example." Announcing that he would no longer accept contributions from single-issue ideological PACs.

src.t: JNS via Cleveland Jewish News

did.text: In 2025 his campaign received $707,803 through AIPAC's PAC ($481,175 in January–June and $226,628 in July–September), the first time in his career he took money from it, according to FEC filings reviewed by Sludge.

src.t: Sludge, Oct. 16, 2025

statements.record: His campaign's itemized PAC receipts fell from $466,530 in 2025 to $34,000 in January–June 2026 (FEC Schedule A, line 11C, reports linked on the Funding tab).

recordSrc.t: FEC filings, Cory Booker for Senate

statements.note: He took substantial money routed through AIPAC's PAC in 2025, then announced a policy against single-issue PAC money in March 2026; his 2026 PAC receipts fit that change, though earmarked flows after September 2025 are not tallied here.

said.text: During his 2019 presidential campaign Hickenlooper said, "I'm not cut out to be a senator," and that he would be a "difficult candidate."

src.t: Cook Political Report, Aug. 30, 2019

did.text: Entered the Colorado Senate race on Aug. 22, 2019: "I know changing Washington is hard, but I want to give it a shot." He won in 2020 and is seeking a second term.

said.text: Colorado's constitutional gift ban (Amendment 41) bars public officials from accepting gifts above a small threshold.

src.t: Colorado Independent Ethics Commission minutes, June 5, 2020

did.text: The Independent Ethics Commission found he violated the gift ban twice in 2018 — a private-jet flight to a submarine commissioning in Connecticut and a Maserati limousine ride at the Bilderberg conference in Italy — and fined him $2,750. His campaign said he "accepts the Commission's findings and takes responsibility."

src.t: The Colorado Sun

statements.note: Documented in the Ethics tab; included here because it is a finding about conduct versus a legal duty.

ethics.title: Colorado ethics commission: two gift-ban violations and a contempt finding
ethics.summary: On a complaint filed by the Public Trust Institute, the Colorado Independent Ethics Commission found that then-Gov. Hickenlooper violated the state's constitutional gift ban by accepting a March 2018 flight on a private jet owned by MDC Holdings CEO Larry Mizel (fine $2,200, 4-0) and a June 2018 Maserati limousine ride at the Bilderberg conference in Turin (fine $550, 4-1). The commission also unanimously held him in contempt after he initially refused to appear at its video hearing; no additional penalty was imposed. Colorado taxpayers paid about $127,000 in attorney fees.
ethics.outcome: $2,750 in fines; contempt finding affirmed. Hickenlooper accepted the findings.

said.text: "I objected to the electoral votes because the Pennsylvania Supreme Court and Governor Tom Wolf repeatedly refused to abide by the Constitution." Perry wrote this in an op-ed explaining his Jan. 6, 2021 objection, citing changes to Pennsylvania's mail-in ballot procedures.

src.t: Broad + Liberty (Perry op-ed)

did.text: Voted Yea on the objection to counting Pennsylvania's electoral votes (House roll call 11, Jan. 7, 2021); the objection failed 138-282.

statements.record: In December 2021, Perry declined a request to cooperate with the House select committee investigating Jan. 6, calling the panel illegitimate.
statements.note: His stated reason for objecting and his recorded vote align; the House rejected the objection.

said.text: "We had the time to act, and this deal fails — fails completely. And that's why these members and others will be absolutely opposed to the deal, and we will do everything in our power to stop it." Perry, then Freedom Caucus chairman, was speaking about the 2023 debt-limit agreement.

src.t: WITF

did.text: Voted Nay on House passage of the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (H.R. 3746), the debt-limit agreement (roll call 243, May 31, 2023).

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 243 (2023)

statements.record: He also voted Nay on the FY2026 consolidated appropriations package (roll call 53, Feb. 3, 2026).

said.text: "I wish I had a nickel for every time the [Freedom Caucus] sounded the alarm and nobody listened, only to find out the hard way we were right all along. We expect MASSIVE improvements from the Senate before it gets back to the House." Perry posted this on X, agreeing with Elon Musk's criticism of the House-passed bill.

src.t: Philadelphia Inquirer

did.text: Voted Yea on final House passage of H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, as amended by the Senate (roll call 190, July 3, 2025).

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 190 (2025)

statements.record: He had also voted Yea on the House version on May 22, 2025 (roll call 145), before posting the criticism, as The Inquirer noted.
statements.note: He publicly criticized the House-passed bill and called for major Senate changes, yet voted for the bill at both stages; whether the final version met his call is a matter of interpretation.

ethics.title: FBI seizure of cellphone in 2020 election investigation
ethics.summary: FBI agents seized Perry's cellphone under a warrant on Aug. 9, 2022, as part of the federal investigation into efforts to overturn the 2020 election, later led by special counsel Jack Smith. Perry argued the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause shielded his messages. Chief Judge Beryl Howell ruled on Dec. 28, 2022 that 2,055 records were not protected; the D.C. Circuit sent the case back for narrower review on Sept. 13, 2023; and Chief Judge James Boasberg ruled on Dec. 19, 2023 that prosecutors could access 1,659 records while 396 were privileged.
ethics.outcome: Perry was not charged with any crime; CNN reported in December 2023 that it was not clear whether he was still under investigation. No charges against him have been documented.

sources.t: Axios (Aug. 9, 2022)
Levin Center: Scott Perry cellphone case

ethics.title: Jan. 6 committee subpoena and Ethics Committee referral
ethics.summary: In December 2021 Perry declined a request to cooperate with the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack, calling it illegitimate, and the committee later subpoenaed him. On Dec. 19, 2022, the committee referred Perry, along with Reps. Kevin McCarthy, Jim Jordan and Andy Biggs, to the House Ethics Committee for failing to comply with its subpoenas.
ethics.outcome: CBS News reported at the time that the referrals were not likely to lead to action with Republicans taking the House majority; this research found no public Ethics Committee action on the referral.

sources.t: CBS News (Dec. 19, 2022)
Roll Call (Dec. 21, 2021)

said.text: "With House leadership refusing to bring any proposal to the floor, I am signing another discharge petition to force a vote and prevent higher health care costs for families in the Hudson Valley." Lawler's office said this was the third discharge petition he had signed on extending the enhanced ACA credits.

src.t: Office of Rep. Lawler

did.text: Voted Yea on H.R. 1834, a three-year extension of the enhanced ACA premium tax credits brought to the floor by discharge petition (roll call 11, Jan. 8, 2026); it passed 230-196, with 17 Republicans voting yes.

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 11 (2026)

statements.record: ABC News reported that the Senate had failed to reach the 60 votes needed for a three-year extension.
statements.note: He said he was pushing to force a floor vote on extending the credits and then voted for the extension when it came up.

said.text: "That is the deal, and I will not accept a penny less. If the Senate reduces the SALT number, I will vote NO, and the bill will fail in the House." He was responding to a Senate draft that kept the cap at $10,000 after the House-passed bill set it at $40,000.

src.t: Office of Rep. Lawler

did.text: Voted Yea on final House passage of H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, as amended by the Senate (roll call 190, July 3, 2025); he had also voted Yea on the House version on May 22, 2025 (roll call 145).

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 190 (2025)

statements.record: Lawler's office said the final bill set a $40,000 SALT cap that phases down for incomes above $500,000 and rises 1% a year, for five years.
statements.note: The final bill kept the $40,000 cap figure he had demanded, and he voted for it.

said.text: "We are in the most precarious circumstances since the lead up to World War 2, which is why it is imperative that we get aid to our Democratic allies in Ukraine, Israel, and Taiwan." He said this when signing a 2024 discharge petition for H.R. 7372, an aid and border-security bill.

src.t: Office of Rep. Lawler

did.text: Voted Yea on H.R. 2913, the Ukraine Support Act, brought to the floor by discharge petition (roll call 207, June 4, 2026).

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 207 (2026)

statements.record: Forbes reported that H.R. 2913 authorizes $1.3 billion in defense aid and $8 billion in direct loans to Ukraine, along with new sanctions on Russia.
statements.note: His stated support for Ukraine aid matches his vote for the 2026 Ukraine Support Act.

said.text: "It is paramount that Congress preserve access to this program for those who need it the most by ensuring that states and the federal government implement commonsense policies to prevent waste, fraud, and abuse in the system." From his statement introducing H.Res. 620, a resolution celebrating Medicaid's 60th anniversary.

src.t: Rep. Evans press release

did.text: Voted YES on final House passage of H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed 218-214 on July 3, 2025 and became law; he also voted YES on initial House passage on May 22, 2025 (215-214-1, roll 145).

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 190 (2025)

statements.record: KFF reports that the Congressional Budget Office estimated the enacted law reduces federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion over 2025-2034.
statements.note: Evans describes the law's eligibility checks and work requirements as protecting Medicaid, while CBO projects the same law lowers federal Medicaid spending by about $911 billion over ten years.

said.text: "open to supporting a common-sense bill that puts necessary guardrails in place and gradually phases out these subsidies, but this is not it." From his written statement on the three-year extension of enhanced ACA premium tax credits.

src.t: Colorado Public Radio

did.text: Voted NO on H.R. 1834, a three-year extension of the enhanced ACA premium tax credits brought to the floor by a discharge petition; it passed the House 230-196 on January 8, 2026, with 17 Republicans voting yes.

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 11 (2026)

statements.record: On Dec. 17, 2025 he voted YES on the House-passed Lower Health Care Premiums for All Americans Act (H.R. 6703), a Republican health bill whose provisions include funding ACA cost-sharing reduction payments starting in 2027, pharmacy benefit manager disclosure and expanded association health plans.
statements.note: His NO vote matches his stated position that he would back only a version with added guardrails and a phase-out, and he supported a separate Republican health-cost bill instead.

said.text: "The focus from a public safety, from a national security lens must remain on deploying all available resources to find these 600,000 plus criminals." Urging ICE not to spend resources on immigrants without criminal records.

src.t: CBS Colorado

did.text: Joined Reps. Salazar and Escobar as one of 20 original cosponsors of the bipartisan DIGNITY Act of 2025, which would let certain undocumented immigrants obtain legal work authorization.

src.t: Rep. Salazar press release

statements.record: His first bill, the UPLIFT Act (announced Feb. 27, 2025), sought to counter Colorado's sanctuary-state laws by allowing local officials to share information with federal immigration authorities and clarifying ICE detainer authority.
statements.note: His record pairs enforcement measures aimed at people with criminal records and sanctuary policies with support for a legal-status pathway for other undocumented immigrants, matching his stated priorities.

ethics.title: Complaint over financial disclosure reports
ethics.summary: The Iowa Democratic Party filed a complaint with the Office of Congressional Ethics alleging Miller-Meeks failed to properly report income on her financial disclosures, including nearly $35,000 from her state pension and Great River Health Systems in 2020, and failed to disclose assets. Her office said it was "working with the House Ethics Committee and House Clerk's office on several substantive questions to resolve the discrepancies" and planned to file an amended report.
ethics.outcome: No public OCE referral or House Ethics Committee action on the complaint was found.

sources.t: WOI (We Are Iowa)
WHO 13

ethics.title: Ethics request over voter-registration address
ethics.summary: A LeClaire, Iowa, resident asked the Office of Congressional Ethics to review Miller-Meeks's residency, alleging she lived primarily in Ottumwa (outside IA-01) while registered to vote at a Scott County address. Her campaign called the complaint "frivolous"; members of Congress are not required to live in the district they represent.
ethics.outcome: In November 2024 Scott County's absentee board accepted and counted her residency-challenged ballot. She changed her voter registration to her Ottumwa home in July 2025, and no OCE action on the request has been reported.

ethics.title: 2020 election contest by Rita Hart
ethics.summary: Miller-Meeks won the 2020 IA-02 race by six votes after a full recount certified by the Iowa State Board of Canvassers, and was provisionally seated on Jan. 3, 2021. Democrat Rita Hart contested the result before the House Administration Committee under the Federal Contested Elections Act, arguing that 22 uncounted ballots would have given her the win. This was a challenge to the election result, not an allegation of misconduct by Miller-Meeks.
ethics.outcome: Hart withdrew her challenge on March 31, 2021; Miller-Meeks kept the seat.

items.title: Stepped down as Senate Human Resources Committee chair
items.summary: Left the Human Resources Committee chairmanship, held since Jan. 14, 2019, and was replaced by Sen. Annette Sweeney; she said she would devote more time to her congressional campaign. In her statement she cited the committee's 2019 work on prescription drug cost transparency, a children's mental health program and Senate passage of behind-the-counter birth control.

bills.title: Appropriations Compliance and Training Act

said.text: "Tariffs are not a strategy. They are a tax on working Americans and the firms that employ them." In the same House floor remarks she called Canada "Ohio's largest fair trade partner that keeps our auto industry strong and globally competitive."

src.t: Congressional Record (House)

did.text: Voted YES on H.J.Res. 72, terminating the national emergency used to impose tariffs on imports from Canada (roll call 65, Feb. 11, 2026); the resolution passed the House.

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 65 (2026)

statements.record: In a March 27, 2025 statement on proposed 25% auto tariffs she said "This will require a lot more than a 25% tariff on automotive imports" and urged negotiated reciprocity agreements with trading partners.
statements.note: Her floor criticism of tariffs and description of Canada as a key fair-trade partner align with her vote to end the Canada tariff emergency.

said.text: "The Power of the Purse rests with Congress." Said when announcing the Appropriations Compliance and Training Act (H.R. 4230) with Rep. Rosa DeLauro to rein in executive-branch spending abuses.

src.t: Office of Rep. Kaptur

did.text: Voted YES on the FY2026 consolidated appropriations package (roll call 53, Feb. 3, 2026).

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 53 (2026)

statements.record: She voted NO on the Nov. 12, 2025 continuing resolution that ended the 2025 government shutdown (roll call 285).
statements.note: As an Appropriations ranking member she sponsored a bill asserting congressional spending authority and voted for full-year FY2026 appropriations, though she opposed the earlier stopgap measure.

ethics.title: Late report of a stock transaction
ethics.summary: In July 2023, Toledo TV stations WTVG (13abc) and WTOL reported that Kaptur was fined $200 for a delay in reporting a stock sale, as required under the STOCK Act's periodic transaction reporting rules. The National Republican Congressional Committee cited the late filing in a memo criticizing her, according to the Washington Examiner.
ethics.outcome: Reported $200 fine; no House Ethics Committee or Office of Congressional Conduct action found.

sources.t: 13abc (WTVG)
WTOL
Washington Examiner

bills.title: Warrior Right to Repair Act of 2025
Establishing the Select Committee on Electoral Reform

said.text: "By preventing Members of Congress from trading stocks, receiving yearly pay raises, and turning to lobbying shortly after their term, more lawmakers will be accountable to their constituents and be in the work of governing for the right reasons." Said when she and Rep. Zach Nunn (R-IA) introduced the No Corruption in Government Act (H.R. 358).

src.t: Office of Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez

did.text: Voted YES on H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act, which also included a photo voter-ID section (roll call 280, July 22, 2026); it passed the House 232-198.

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 280 (2026)

statements.note: She co-introduced a congressional stock-trading ban in 2025 and voted for the House-passed ban in 2026.

said.text: "The pressure to vote in line with your party is just immense in DC." Bloomberg Government reported at the time that she voted with her party 75% of the time on party-line votes, the third-lowest rate among House Democrats.

src.t: Bloomberg Government

did.text: Voted YES on the continuing resolution that ended the 2025 government shutdown (roll call 285, Nov. 12, 2025), which passed while most House Democrats voted NO.

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 285 (2025)

statements.record: In her statement on that vote she said, "I'll work with whoever is necessary to reach those goals – and I don't give a damn which side of the aisle they sit on."
statements.note: Her stated willingness to break from her party matches her vote for the shutdown-ending stopgap that most House Democrats opposed.

said.text: "Our servicemembers need reliable warfighting equipment, and their lives could depend on the ability to repair that equipment quickly when the situation demands." Said when introducing the Warrior Right to Repair Act.

src.t: Office of Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez

did.text: Introduced H.R. 5155, the Warrior Right to Repair Act of 2025, as lead sponsor with bipartisan cosponsors.

src.t: GovInfo bill status, H.R. 5155

statements.record: Her office reported she also co-led the FARM Act (H.R. 5857) on farm-equipment repair with Rep. Joe Neguse in late 2025 and helped introduce the Fair Repair Act on consumer electronics in February 2026.
statements.note: Her public advocacy for right-to-repair is matched by legislation she sponsored and co-led in the 119th Congress.

bills.title: VISIBLE Act (Visible Identification Standards for Immigration-Based Law Enforcement Act of 2025): requires immigration enforcement officers to display visible identification during public-facing enforcement actions
Save American Democracy Act: would prohibit most mid-decade congressional redistricting

statements.topic: 2025 government shutdown and ACA tax credits

said.text: "Right now, costs are too high, and healthcare costs are about to soar because of Republican's failure to renew tax credits that make healthcare more affordable for over 100,000 South Texans." Statement issued as the federal shutdown began.

src.t: Rep. Gonzalez press release

did.text: Voted NO on the continuing resolution that ended the 2025 government shutdown (House roll call 285, Nov. 12, 2025); the measure passed the House.

src.t: House Clerk roll call 285

statements.record: On Nov. 24, 2025, his office said he had signed a discharge petition to force a House vote on a three-year extension of the ACA premium tax credits.
statements.note: He tied his shutdown position to renewing the health-care tax credits, voted against the funding bill that ended the shutdown, and then backed a discharge petition seeking a vote on extending those credits.

said.text: "Across the country, redistricting has turned into a political weapon that allows both parties to choose their voters instead of the voters choosing their leaders." Said when announcing his bill to prohibit mid-decade redistricting.

src.t: Rep. Gonzalez press release

did.text: Introduced H.R. 5879, the Save American Democracy Act, which would prohibit most mid-decade congressional redistricting; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.

src.t: GovInfo bill status, H.R. 5879

statements.note: His stated opposition to mid-decade redistricting matches the bill he introduced to restrict it.

said.text: "Warrantless immigration raids on private properties are setting a dangerous, unconstitutional precedent in this country—not just for immigrant families, but for every American family." Said when introducing the Say No to Warrantless Searches Act.

src.t: Rep. Gonzalez press release

did.text: Voted YES on the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with certain crimes such as theft; it passed the House 263-156 (House roll call 23, Jan. 22, 2025).

src.t: House Clerk roll call 23

statements.record: He also introduced H.R. 4667, the VISIBLE Act (July 23, 2025), which would require immigration enforcement officers to display visible identification during public-facing enforcement actions.
statements.note: He voted to expand mandatory detention of immigrants charged with certain crimes while sponsoring bills to limit how immigration enforcement is carried out, so his record combines support for some enforcement measures with limits on others.

ethics.outcome: The trade was disclosed, late, in June 2022. No House Ethics Committee action or penalty beyond the standard late-filing process was reported in the coverage reviewed.

members.roles: House Energy and Commerce Committee; Ranking Member, Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy; Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade; Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Communications and Technology; Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party; Co-chair, Congressional Special Operations Forces (SOF) Caucus

bills.title: Florida Coastal Protection Act: would bar oil and gas exploration, development, and production in certain Outer Continental Shelf areas off Florida
Keep Kids Covered Act: would provide continuous Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for certain children

statements.topic: Voter ID and the SAVE Act

said.text: "H.R. 8281 the 'SAVE Act' is an extreme attempt to suppress voting by requiring a birth certificate – not a military id or driver's license — to register to vote." From an undated constituent e-newsletter about the 2024 version of the SAVE Act, which the House passed in July 2024.

src.t: Rep. Castor e-newsletter

did.text: Voted YES on H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act (House roll call 280, July 22, 2026). The bill bars members of Congress from buying new stocks and, as passed by the House, also requires voters to show photo ID when voting in federal elections. It passed 232-198.

src.t: House Clerk roll call 280

statements.record: She voted NO on the 2025 SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote (House roll call 102, Apr. 10, 2025). ABC News reported that House Republicans added the voter-ID language to the stock-trading bill and that many Democrats objected to it.
statements.note: She opposed the SAVE Act's proof-of-citizenship requirement for registering to vote but voted for a stock-trading bill that also contained a photo-ID requirement for voting; the two measures differ, and her 2024 statement singled out birth-certificate requirements rather than driver's licenses.

said.text: "Dangerous offshore drilling can devastate both our environment and our economy, posing huge risks to everything that makes Florida special." Said when introducing the bipartisan Florida Coastal Protection Act.

src.t: Rep. Castor press release

did.text: Introduced H.R. 2673, the Florida Coastal Protection Act, which would bar oil and gas exploration, development, and production in certain Outer Continental Shelf areas off Florida; it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee.

src.t: GovInfo bill status, H.R. 2673

statements.note: Her stated opposition to offshore drilling near Florida matches the bill she sponsored to prohibit it.

said.text: "Ratepayers should not have to subsidize wealthy corporations' growing energy demands, especially from AI data centers." Said when announcing a bipartisan bill on data-center electricity costs.

src.t: Rep. Castor press release

did.text: Co-led the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act with Rep. Gabe Evans (R-CO). The bill aims to keep households from paying higher electric bills tied to data-center development.

src.t: Rep. Castor press release

statements.record: Castor's office announced House passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act on Sept. 16, 2026.
statements.note: Her statement on data-center energy costs matches the bill she co-led, which later passed the House.

ethics.title: Late disclosure of 2021 stock purchases
ethics.summary: Business Insider listed Castor among members of Congress who violated the STOCK Act's disclosure deadlines, reporting that she "was late disclosing the purchase of tens of thousands of dollars worth of stock shares throughout 2021." The report did not include a response from her office.
ethics.outcome: The coverage reviewed reported no House Ethics Committee or Office of Congressional Ethics action.

sources.t: Business Insider (via Yahoo Finance), STOCK Act violations list

members.ethicsSearched: Searched for STOCK Act late-disclosure reports (Business Insider and other news coverage, stock-trade trackers), House Ethics Committee and Office of Congressional Ethics matters, and criminal or civil cases involving Rep. Castor; only the Business Insider late-disclosure listing was documented by a credible outlet (partisan reports from the NRCC and Florida's Voice repeating the issue were not used as sources).

bill.officialTitle: A bill to protect a person's ability to determine whether to continue or end a pregnancy, and to protect a health care provider's ability to provide abortion services.

src.t: NPR via Texas Public Radio, 'Negotiators release $118 billion border bill as GOP leaders call it dead in the House' (Feb. 4, 2024)

src.t: Reuters via KSL.com, 'Senate defeats border deal, but Ukraine, Israel aid may survive' (Feb. 7, 2024)

src.t: CNN, Senate vote on Israel and Ukraine aid (Apr. 23, 2024)

hvotes.question: On passage

bill.officialTitle: To provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14.
bill.summary: This budget reconciliation law reduces taxes, reduces or increases spending for various federal programs, increases the statutory debt limit, and otherwise addresses agencies and programs throughout the federal government. It includes legislation submitted by congressional committees under the FY2025 budget resolution (H. Con. Res. 14) and was considered under expedited reconciliation procedures that prevent a filibuster in the Senate (CRS summary).

summarySrc.t: CRS summary of H.R. 1 (119th Congress), Public Law version, GovInfo bill-summary XML

provisions.fact: Medicaid: CBO estimates the Medicaid provisions in P.L. 119-21 will reduce federal outlays by $989.7 billion (and reduce revenues by $25.9 billion) over FY2025-FY2034, and increase the number of people without health insurance by 7.5 million in FY2034 (CRS report R48633, Aug. 18, 2025).

src.t: Congressional Research Service, 'Health Provisions in P.L. 119-21, the FY2025 Reconciliation Law' (R48633), via EveryCRSReport

provisions.fact: 2017 individual tax cuts: the law makes permanent the individual income tax rates that the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) instituted through 2025, and makes permanent (and further raises) the TCJA's increase to the standard deduction (CRS report R48611, July 29, 2025).

src.t: Congressional Research Service, 'Tax Provisions in P.L. 119-21, the FY2025 Reconciliation Law' (R48611), via EveryCRSReport

provisions.fact: Clean-energy credits: the law makes changes to a number of energy-related tax provisions, including early termination of many energy-related tax incentives such as the tax credits for clean vehicles and the production and investment tax credits for clean electricity (CRS report R48611).

src.t: Congressional Research Service, 'Tax Provisions in P.L. 119-21, the FY2025 Reconciliation Law' (R48611), via EveryCRSReport

provisions.fact: Immigration enforcement: according to NPR, the law provides about $170 billion for border and immigration enforcement goals, including roughly $46.5 billion to complete the border wall, $45 billion for immigration detention centers and about $30 billion to hire more ICE personnel.

src.t: NPR (Juliana Kim) via GPB, 'How Trump's big beautiful bill aims to supercharge immigration enforcement' (July 2025)

codes.why: CBO estimates its Medicaid provisions reduce federal outlays by $989.7 billion over 2025–2034 (CRS report R48633).
It makes the 2017 individual tax-rate cuts permanent (CRS report R48611) while reducing spending on some programs.

It provides about $170 billion for border and immigration enforcement, including detention centers and ICE hiring (NPR).

record.title: 2025 quorum break over mid-decade congressional redistricting
record.detail: Joined House Democrats who left Texas to deny the House a quorum and delay a vote on a new Republican-drawn congressional map (HB 4). Democrats returned on Aug. 18; the House passed the map 88–52 on Aug. 20 and it was signed on Aug. 29, 2025. record.title: Suit against New York doctor over abortion pills
record.detail: In December 2024 Paxton sued New York physician Margaret Carpenter in Collin County, the first Texas suit against an out-of-state abortion-pill prescriber; in February 2025 a Texas judge ordered her to pay more than $100,000 in penalties. The Ulster County, N.Y., clerk refused to file the judgment under New York's shield law, and on Oct. 31, 2025 a New York judge dismissed Paxton's petition to compel enforcement.

record.title: Remain in Mexico lawsuit (Biden v. Texas)
record.detail: Texas and Missouri sued to force the Biden administration to keep the 'Remain in Mexico' asylum policy and won in lower courts; on June 30, 2022 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 5–4 for the administration, holding that ending the program did not violate federal immigration law.

record.title: Election-crime prosecutions limited by state's highest criminal court
record.detail: In State v. Stephens, the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals ruled 8–1 that the attorney general cannot unilaterally prosecute election crimes without a request from a local district or county attorney; it reaffirmed the ruling 7–2 in September 2022 after Paxton sought rehearing. By March 2023, cases against at least seven people accused of 152 election offenses had been dismissed or were awaiting dismissal.

src.t: Texas Tribune: Texas AG Ken Paxton's election crime cases face dismissal after ruling (Mar. 15, 2023)

record.title: Challenge to the Affordable Care Act (California v. Texas)
record.detail: Texas led a 20-state coalition that sued in 2018 arguing the ACA was unconstitutional after Congress set the individual-mandate penalty to $0; the federal district court held the entire law invalid. On June 17, 2021 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that Texas and the other plaintiff states lacked standing, leaving the ACA in place.

ethics.title: 2015 state securities-fraud indictment
ethics.summary: A Collin County grand jury indicted Paxton in July 2015 on three felony counts (two first-degree, one third-degree) related to securities dealings before he became attorney general; he pleaded not guilty. On March 26, 2024, on the eve of trial, he entered a pretrial intervention agreement without a plea, agreeing to pay about $271,000 in restitution, perform 100 hours of community service and take 15 hours of legal-ethics courses.
ethics.outcome: Charges dismissed June 18, 2025 after he completed the pretrial intervention terms; no conviction or admission of guilt.

sources.t: Texas Tribune: Felony charges against Ken Paxton to be dropped (Mar. 26, 2024)

ethics.title: 2023 impeachment by the Texas House
ethics.summary: The Texas House voted 121–23 to impeach Paxton on 20 articles, mostly alleging he abused his office to help political donor Nate Paul, along with articles tied to the securities case and general misconduct; he was suspended from office pending trial. The Senate tried 16 articles in September 2023, with 21 votes needed to convict.
ethics.outcome: Acquitted on all 16 articles on Sept. 16, 2023 (no article drew more than 14 votes to convict); the Senate voted 19–11 to dismiss the four remaining articles, and he returned to office.

sources.t: Ballotpedia: Impeachment of Ken Paxton, 2023
Texas Tribune: Attorney general acquitted on 16 impeachment counts (Sept. 16, 2023)

ethics.title: Whistleblower lawsuit by former top aides
ethics.summary: Four former senior aides sued under the Texas Whistleblower Act in November 2020, alleging they were fired after reporting Paxton to the FBI over his dealings with Nate Paul. A $3.3 million settlement Paxton agreed to in February 2023 was not funded by the Legislature, prompting the House investigation. In April 2025 Travis County District Judge Catherine Mauzy ruled the office violated the Whistleblower Act and ordered $6.6 million in damages and fees.
ethics.outcome: Paxton dropped his appeal on July 2, 2025, leaving the $6.6 million judgment in place, to be paid by the state.

sources.t: KUT: Texas will pay $6.6 million to whistleblowers after Paxton drops appeal (July 4, 2025)
KUT: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's former aides win $6.6 million in whistleblower case (Apr. 5, 2025)

ethics.title: Federal investigation of aides' bribery and abuse-of-office allegations
ethics.summary: After eight top aides reported Paxton to the FBI in 2020 over alleged help for donor Nate Paul, federal authorities investigated possible bribery and abuse of office; the case was moved to the Justice Department's Public Integrity Section in Washington in 2023. Paul later pleaded guilty to making false statements to lenders in a separate federal case.
ethics.outcome: Closed without charges: the Justice Department decided in the final weeks of the Biden administration (reported April 3, 2025) not to prosecute, with a senior career official citing doubts a conviction could be obtained.

sources.t: PBS NewsHour/AP: DOJ declined to prosecute Texas attorney general in final weeks of Biden's term (Apr. 3, 2025)

ethics.title: State Bar of Texas disciplinary lawsuit over 2020 election suit
ethics.summary: The bar's Commission for Lawyer Discipline sued Paxton in May 2022, alleging 'dishonest representations' about voting irregularities in his Texas v. Pennsylvania filing. A divided state appeals court let the case proceed in 2024, but in December 2024 the Texas Supreme Court ruled for his first assistant, Brent Webster, in a parallel case, and the commission moved to drop its suit against Paxton in January 2025.
ethics.outcome: Dismissed: the Texas Supreme Court dismissed the case as moot and vacated the appeals-court ruling on Feb. 14, 2025; no discipline was imposed.

record.title: Platform: Medicare for All, no corporate money
record.detail: Campaigned on the message "Money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for All," backing a government single-payer health system, rejecting corporate PAC donations and calling for abolishing ICE; his campaign site states it is funded by individuals, "not corporations."

record.title: Position on U.S. arms sales to Israel
record.detail: In the Democratic primary debate, said the U.S. should stop selling weapons to Israel, which he accused of "human rights abuses, genocide and apartheid," and criticized AIPAC's influence on U.S. foreign policy.

src.t: CBS News: Democrats Stevens and El-Sayed clash over Israel and campaign money in tense Michigan Senate primary debate (Jul. 7, 2026)

record.title: Launched U.S. Senate campaign
record.detail: Formally launched his campaign for the seat held by retiring Sen. Gary Peters after leaving his Wayne County post, focusing on health care costs, housing, child care and "breaking the corporate chokehold on our economy."

record.title: Wayne County medical debt relief program
record.detail: His department launched a county contract (approved by the county commission in early March 2024; $5 million over two years from the indigent health fund and federal ARPA money) with the nonprofit RIP Medical Debt to buy and cancel up to $700 million in medical debt for about 300,000 residents; by June 2026 about $57.4 million had been cleared for 83,291 residents (Bridge Michigan).

record.title: Juvenile detention public health emergency
record.detail: As Wayne County health officer, signed with County Executive Warren Evans a public health emergency order for the overcrowded, understaffed Wayne County Juvenile Detention Facility (population had risen from an average of 68 in 2021 to 137); the county lifted the emergency on June 5, 2023 after hiring 54 staff and raising wages 35% (BridgeDetroit).

src.t: Michigan Public: Wayne County CEO calls for a Public Health State of Emergency at Wayne County Juvenile Detention Facility (Mar. 22, 2023)

record.title: Lead testing of Detroit school water

ethics.title: Challenge to eligibility for 2018 governor's race
ethics.summary: Rival Democratic candidate Shri Thanedar and others challenged El-Sayed's eligibility because he had registered to vote in New York while in medical school, citing Michigan's requirement that candidates be qualified electors for four years. El-Sayed also asked a court to rule on his eligibility.
ethics.outcome: The Michigan Bureau of Elections dismissed the challenges, finding he had been continuously registered in Michigan since 2003; the Court of Claims dismissed El-Sayed's own suit, and he stayed on the ballot.

ethics.outcome: Report filed July 28, 2026; no ethics or FEC complaint was reported in the coverage reviewed.

cands.since: Former Governor of North Carolina (January 2017 – January 2025)
cands.roles: Governor of North Carolina, 2017–2025; North Carolina Attorney General, 2001–2017; North Carolina Senate, 1991–2001 (Majority Leader 1997–2001); North Carolina House of Representatives, 1987–1991
cands.background: Lawyer from Nashville, North Carolina, who practiced at a family law firm before entering the state legislature; served nearly 16 years as attorney general and two terms as governor, then took a teaching position at Harvard University after leaving office.

record.title: Commuted 15 death sentences
record.detail: On his final day in office, commuted the death sentences of 15 people to life without parole after a clemency review; 121 people remained on North Carolina's death row.

src.t: WUNC: Roy Cooper commutes 15 death row sentences on his final day in office

record.title: Vetoed HB 10 (school vouchers and sheriff-ICE cooperation)
record.detail: Vetoed House Bill 10, which expanded Opportunity Scholarship private-school voucher funding and required sheriffs to honor ICE detainer requests for up to 48 hours; he called the vouchers 'the biggest threat to public schools in decades.' The legislature overrode the veto (House 72-44 on Nov. 19, Senate on Nov. 20, 2024).

src.t: WUNC: Gov. Cooper vetoes bill funding private school vouchers and requiring sheriffs' ICE cooperation

record.title: Vetoed SB 20 (12-week abortion limit)
record.detail: Vetoed Senate Bill 20, which reduced the abortion limit from 20 to 12 weeks with exceptions and added new requirements on providers and patients. The Republican supermajority overrode the veto on May 16, 2023, and the bill became law.

src.t: Office of the Governor: Governor Cooper Vetoes SB20

record.title: Signed Medicaid expansion (HB 76)
record.detail: Signed House Bill 76 (Access to Healthcare Options), making North Carolina the 40th state to expand Medicaid, with coverage expected to reach more than 600,000 residents; enrollment began in December 2023.

src.t: Office of the Governor: Governor Cooper Signs Medicaid Expansion into Law

record.title: Statewide COVID-19 Stay at Home order (EO 121)
record.detail: Issued Executive Order 121, a statewide Stay at Home order requiring residents to stay home except for essential activities and limiting gatherings to 10 people, in effect from March 30 to April 29, 2020.

src.t: NC Department of Public Safety: Governor Cooper Announces Statewide Stay at Home Order Until April 29

record.title: Signed HB 142 repealing HB2 ('bathroom bill')
record.detail: Signed a negotiated compromise that repealed HB2's bathroom restrictions but made the legislature the sole authority over restroom access and barred local regulation of private employment and public accommodations until December 1, 2020.

src.t: Ballotpedia: Did Gov. Roy Cooper betray promises on HB 2 repeal?

record.title: As attorney general, dropped Duke lacrosse charges
record.detail: After taking over the prosecution from Durham DA Mike Nifong, dismissed all charges against three Duke lacrosse players and declared them innocent, citing a 'tragic rush to accuse.'

src.t: GoDuke.com: N.C. Attorney General Roy Cooper's Statement

ethics.title: Atlantic Coast Pipeline mitigation fund investigation
ethics.summary: Investigators hired by the Republican-led Joint Legislative Commission on Governmental Operations concluded that Cooper improperly used his authority to secure a $57.8 million mitigation-fund commitment from pipeline developers while a state permit was pending; the report found he did not personally benefit. Cooper called the probe partisan and denied wrongdoing, and Duke Energy and state environmental officials said they did not feel coerced.
ethics.outcome: No charges or formal sanctions; the legislature redirected the fund to schools in pipeline-route counties.

sources.t: WUNC: Investigation Finds Gov. Cooper Improperly Controlled $58M Pipeline Fund
WRAL: Report: Cooper didn't benefit from pipeline actions, but investigators suggest improper influence

ethics.title: Libel suit over 2000 attorney general campaign ad (Boyce & Isley v. Cooper)
ethics.summary: Lawyers Dan Boyce (Cooper's 2000 Republican opponent), Gene Boyce and the Isleys sued Cooper over a 2000 campaign ad that implied they acted unethically in seeking attorney fees in a class-action tax case. The case ran for about 14 years before settling.
ethics.outcome: Settled in April 2014 for $75,000 plus mediator fees and a written apology signed by Cooper stating that to the extent the ad implied otherwise, "we were wrong and apologize."

sources.t: WRAL: Cooper settles libel suit from 2000 election

record.title: RNC Michigan voter-roll lawsuit dismissed
record.detail: The RNC under Whatley sued Michigan's secretary of state in March 2024 alleging failure to remove ineligible people from voter rolls; U.S. District Judge Jane Beckering dismissed the suit, finding the plaintiffs lacked standing and had not identified any specific ineligible voter on the active rolls.

src.t: WILX: Federal judge dismisses RNC lawsuit over Michigan voter records

record.title: Sued NC elections board over 225,000 registrations
record.detail: As RNC chair, joined the North Carolina GOP in suing the State Board of Elections under the Help America Vote Act over about 225,000 registrations lacking a driver's license number or partial Social Security number, seeking removal or provisional ballots. The case was settled in February 2026 without a purge: the state agreed to continue its registration-repair effort and to reject future applications lacking the required ID information.

src.t: Carolina Journal: Judge approves RNC, DNC, elections board deal ending registration case

record.title: Launched RNC-Trump campaign 'election integrity' program
record.detail: Announced, with the Trump campaign, a program of more than 100,000 volunteers and attorneys to monitor elections; the RNC said it had filed 82 election-related lawsuits in 25 states at that point.

src.t: RNC: Trump Campaign and RNC Unveil Historic 100,000 Person Strong Election Integrity Program

record.title: First RNC strategy memo as chair
record.detail: Days after being elected RNC chair on March 8, 2024, issued a memo prioritizing turnout, coordination with the Trump campaign and an 'aggressive' election-litigation posture, including early-voting and mail-ballot programs; more than 60 RNC staff were let go during the leadership transition.

src.t: NPR: As Trump continues to remake RNC in his image, new memo outlines what that looks like

record.title: NC GOP challenge to absentee-ballot deadline extension
record.detail: As state party chair, the North Carolina Republican Party joined the Trump campaign and the RNC (Wise v. Circosta) in asking the U.S. Supreme Court to block a State Board of Elections settlement extending the mail-ballot receipt deadline to Nov. 12, 2020; the Court declined, with three justices dissenting.

src.t: SCOTUSblog: Court won't block extended deadline for North Carolina mail-in ballots

record.title: RIFLE Act (H.R. 2552)

record.title: Trade crimes enforcement bill (H.R. 1869)
record.detail: Sponsored the Protecting American Industry and Labor from International Trade Crimes Act, which would create a dedicated Justice Department Criminal Division structure to investigate and prosecute trade crimes and require annual Attorney General reports to Congress; co-led by Reps. did.text: Voted against the infrastructure bill (H.R. 3684) in the House, saying it added too much spending beyond physical infrastructure without being fully paid for.

statements.record: On Dec. 10, 2021, after the law passed, Hinson joined a bipartisan letter asking the Army Corps to direct the funds to Upper Mississippi lock and dam projects.
statements.note: She opposed the bill's passage but later sought and claimed credit for Iowa's share of its funding; PolitiFact rated a critic's claim that she did so Mostly True.

said.text: "I don't trade stocks and no one else in Congress should either," Hinson says in a 2026 campaign ad, adding, "I voted to ban it."

src.t: KCRG: Fact check: Did Ashley Hinson vote to ban stock trading in Congress?

did.text: Voted Yea on House passage of the Stop Insider Trading Act (H.R. 7008), which passed 232–198 (Roll Call 280).

src.t: Clerk of the House: Roll Call 280, H.R. 7008

statements.record: KCRG found Hinson sold her publicly traded stocks after taking office in 2021, while her family holds $1 million–$5 million in private stock from the sale of her husband's insurance business; the bill exempts pre-existing and private holdings and awaits Senate action.
statements.note: KCRG confirmed she voted for the House-passed bill, which restricts members' stock purchases but does not bar all holdings.

did.text: Voted Nay on H.Con.Res. 93, directing the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities with Iran; it passed 220–204 (Roll Call 307).

src.t: Clerk of the House: Roll Call 307, H.Con.Res. 93

statements.record: Iowa Public Radio reported this was the seventh time she voted against a resolution directing the president to end the conflict.
statements.note: She called for the war to end a week after voting against a congressional directive to withdraw forces; the cited reports include no explanation from her of how the two positions relate.

ethics.title: Plagiarized passages on 2020 campaign website
ethics.summary: The New York Times reported that pages on Hinson's 2020 House campaign website copied passages word-for-word from news outlets including the Times, the Des Moines Register and The Hill. Hinson said she was unaware of the copying when reviewing drafts from staff and said, "As a journalist I take this extremely seriously and am deeply sorry for the mistake."
ethics.outcome: Campaign removed passages and Hinson apologized, saying responsible staff would be held accountable; no formal complaint or penalty documented.

cands.name: Chris Pappas
cands.status: Democratic nominee; won the September 8, 2026 primary with 62% to Karishma Manzur's 27% (NHPR) for the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen

statusSrc.t: NHPR: Pappas, Sununu win Senate primaries in New Hampshire (Sept. 8, 2026)

cands.since: U.S. Representative, New Hampshire's 1st District (since January 2019)
cands.roles: U.S. House of Representatives (NH-01), 2019–present; New Hampshire Executive Council, District 4, 2013–2019; Hillsborough County Treasurer, 2007–2011; New Hampshire House of Representatives, 2003–2007
cands.background: Co-owner of the Puritan Backroom, a Manchester restaurant founded by his great-grandfather in 1917 and a frequent stop for presidential candidates. He holds a bachelor's degree in government from Harvard College (2002).
cands.term: Running for an open Senate seat

record.title: DISCLOSE Act of 2026 (H.R. 7802)
record.detail: Introduced the House version of the DISCLOSE Act with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse. The bill would require super PACs, dark-money groups and other organizations spending more than $10,000 on elections to disclose donors giving more than $10,000. It would also extend disclosure rules to online ads and paid social-media influencers. His office said 139 House Democrats and 47 Democratic senators joined the House and Senate versions. The sources reviewed show no committee or floor action.

src.t: Office of Rep. Chris Pappas: Pappas, Whitehouse Reintroduce Updated DISCLOSE Act (Mar. 4, 2026)

record.title: PFAS Research and Development Reauthorization Act of 2025 (H.R. 6667)
record.detail: Introduced a bill to extend the authorization of appropriations for EPA research and development on PFAS ("forever chemicals"). It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Science, and Transportation and Infrastructure committees.

src.t: GovInfo: H.R. 6667 (IH), 119th Congress

record.title: Discharge petition for congressional stock-trading ban (H.R. 5106)
record.detail: Was among the first members to sign a discharge petition to force a House vote on the bipartisan Restore Trust in Congress Act (H.R. 5106), which he cosponsored. His office reported in July 2026 that he voted for a House-passed ban on stock trading by members of Congress.

src.t: Office of Rep. Chris Pappas: Pappas Votes to Ban Stock Trading by Members of Congress (July 22, 2026)

record.title: Accelerating Home Building Act (H.R. 5907)
record.detail: Co-led, with Reps. Janelle Bynum, Bryan Steil and Brian Fitzpatrick, a bill creating a HUD grant program to fund "pattern books" of pre-approved housing designs. His office reported that the bill was included in the amended ROAD to Housing package the House passed in May 2026.

src.t: Office of Rep. Chris Pappas: Major Housing Bill Passes with Pappas Provisions (May 20, 2026)

record.title: Keep the Heat On Act of 2025 (H.R. 5687)
record.detail: Introduced a bill that would appropriate funds for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) during a federal shutdown. It was referred to the House Appropriations Committee.

src.t: GovInfo: H.R. 5687 (IH), 119th Congress

said.text: "The DISCLOSE Act would stop billionaires and corporate special interests from secretly buying our elections by requiring dark money groups to disclose who their donors are." Pappas said this when he reintroduced the bill.

src.t: Office of Rep. Chris Pappas press release (Mar. 4, 2026)

did.text: Is the lead House sponsor of H.R. 7802, the DISCLOSE Act of 2026. He first cosponsored the DISCLOSE Act in 2019.

src.t: New Hampshire Bulletin: Pappas is making campaign finance part of his US Senate bid (Sept. 3, 2026)

statements.record: Pappas says he does not take corporate PAC money. Both primary opponents, Karishma Manzur and Scott Brown, called his 2026 push late, and the New Hampshire Bulletin reported that he has accepted more than $600,000 from AIPAC over his career.
statements.note: He sponsored the disclosure bill he describes. The bill has not advanced, and critics point to non-corporate PAC money, which his pledge does not cover.

said.text: "For far too long, members of both parties have gotten rich trading stocks using insider information they got while holding public office, and thousands of my constituents are demanding we put a stop to this corrupt practice."

src.t: Office of Rep. Chris Pappas: Pappas Votes to Ban Stock Trading by Members of Congress (July 22, 2026)

did.text: Signed the discharge petition for the Restore Trust in Congress Act (H.R. 5106), which he cosponsors, on December 2, 2025. He also cosponsors the TRUST in Congress Act (H.R. 396), and his office says he voted for the House-passed ban in July 2026.

src.t: Pappas for Senate: ICYMI: Congressman Chris Pappas Leads Efforts to Ban Congressional Stock Trading

statements.note: His cosponsorships, discharge-petition signature and reported vote match his stated position.

said.text: "No family should ever wonder if they can afford to keep their home warm during the winter months." Pappas said this when he announced energy-cost bills, including a reauthorization of the Weatherization Assistance Program.

src.t: Office of Rep. Chris Pappas: Pappas Announces New Legislation to Reduce Energy Costs (Jan. 16, 2026)

did.text: Sponsored H.R. 5687, the Keep the Heat On Act, to keep LIHEAP heating aid funded during a government shutdown. It was referred to the Appropriations Committee.

src.t: GovInfo: H.R. 5687 (IH)

statements.note: He filed legislation matching the stated goal; the sources reviewed show no committee action on it.

ethics.title: 2002 Election Day phone-jamming by New Hampshire GOP operatives
ethics.summary: On Election Day 2002, during Sununu's first Senate race, about 800 hang-up calls jammed Democratic get-out-the-vote phone lines in New Hampshire. The state Republican Party's executive director, who paid a Virginia telemarketing firm, and that firm's president pleaded guilty. Republican operative James Tobin was convicted in 2005; a federal appeals court overturned his conviction in March 2007.
ethics.outcome: Two guilty pleas with prison sentences; one conviction overturned on appeal (2007). State and national Republicans paid $135,000 to settle the Democrats' civil suit (December 2006). The sources reviewed report no charges against Sununu or his campaign.

sources.t: Bush campaigner's conviction in New Hampshire phone jamming case overturned (JURIST, March 22, 2007)

record.title: R3 grants: $45 million to 148 programs
record.detail: The Restore, Reinvest and Renew (R3) program, whose board the Lt. Governor's office lists Stratton as leading, announced $45 million in cannabis-revenue grants to 148 programs in civil legal aid, economic development, reentry, violence prevention and youth development; the JEO report puts total R3 awards through 2022 at nearly $150 million to more than 300 organizations.

src.t: Illinois R3: ICJIA Awards $45 Million in R3 Program Grants (June 23, 2022)

record.title: State ID pilot for people leaving prison
record.detail: The JEO Initiative she leads launched a State ID pilot with the Secretary of State and the Illinois Department of Corrections in December 2020; it was expanded to all IDOC facilities by 2022 and had issued over 1,400 state IDs to people returning to their communities, according to the office's 2022 annual report.

src.t: Office of the Lt. Governor: 2022 JEO Annual Report

record.title: Cannabis legalization law (HB 1438)
record.detail: Stratton backed and spoke at the signing of HB 1438, the Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act, which legalized adult-use cannabis from January 1, 2020, made about 700,000 records eligible for expungement, and directed 25% of cannabis revenue to the Restore, Reinvest and Renew (R3) grant program. The governor signed the bill.

src.t: Riverside-Brookfield Landmark: Pritzker signs 'equity-centric' marijuana legalization bill (June 26, 2019)

record.title: Named to lead Justice, Equity and Opportunity Initiative
record.detail: Gov. JB Pritzker's Executive Order 2019-09 created the Justice, Equity and Opportunity (JEO) Initiative to coordinate criminal justice reform across state agencies, with an emphasis on reducing the prison population; Stratton was named to lead it, with annual reports required.

src.t: Capitol News Illinois: Pritzker names Lt. Gov. Stratton to lead criminal justice reform initiative (Feb. 12, 2019)

record.title: HB 2663: ban on expulsions from state-funded preschool
record.detail: As chief House sponsor, Stratton carried HB 2663, which bars expulsion of children from state-funded early childhood programs and requires documented interventions and transition plans instead. It passed the House 95-20 (March 29, 2017) and the Senate 48-0 (May 19, 2017) and was signed by Gov. Bruce Rauner as Public Act 100-0105, effective January 1, 2018.

record.title: Positions on cost of living and President Trump
record.detail: In a general-election interview, Tracy said he is running "to reduce the cost of living for all Illinoisans, especially working families." On President Trump's effect on Illinois races he said, "He's not on the ballot this time," and named no specific policy disagreements, saying he weighs issues "on an issue-by-issue basis." He said the "jury's still out" on tariffs.

src.t: Capitol News Illinois: 'Underdog' Tracy says he's 'answering a call of duty' by running for Durbin's seat (July 7, 2026)

record.title: Economic platform
record.detail: In his Chicago Sun-Times candidate questionnaire, Tracy committed to "rein in inflation by cutting waste, fraud and excessive government spending," pursue "an all-of-the-above energy strategy" and "grow paychecks by reducing excess regulations."

src.t: Chicago Sun-Times candidate questionnaire: Don Tracy

record.title: Immigration enforcement and tariffs
record.detail: On the federal immigration operation in the Chicago area (Operation Midway Blitz), Tracy called for "transparency and oversight on enforcement priorities" and faster immigration-court processing. On trade, he wrote that "tariffs may be an effective tool, especially when used in a targeted, strategic manner to protect Illinois farmers and manufacturers."

src.t: Chicago Sun-Times candidate questionnaire: Don Tracy

record.title: Resigned as Illinois GOP chairman
record.detail: Announced his resignation as state party chairman, effective after the July 2024 Republican National Convention. His letter cited intraparty fighting and the removal of a state central committee member "without due process." He had survived a no-confidence vote in spring 2023 after the party's losses in the 2022 elections.

src.t: Capitol News Illinois: Just weeks before Republican National Convention, Illinois GOP chair announces resignation (June 20, 2024)

record.title: Party challenge to Democratic-drawn legislative maps (McConchie v. Illinois State Board of Elections)
record.detail: While Tracy chaired the party, the Illinois Republican Party was a plaintiff, with GOP legislative leaders Dan McConchie and Jim Durkin and their caucuses, in a federal suit first filed June 9, 2021 against the June 2021 legislative redistricting plan. A three-judge federal court declared the June plan unconstitutional because of its population deviations and enjoined it. The court then used the legislature's revised September 2021 plan as the starting point for the final map.

ethics.title: Inspector general finding on political contribution while Gaming Board chairman
ethics.summary: In 2019 the Illinois Executive Inspector General found that Tracy had engaged in prohibited political activity by making a $1,000 campaign contribution to a Republican legislative candidate while chairing the Illinois Gaming Board, a post that bars such contributions. Tracy said his wife made the contribution on her own from a joint account. He sued to obtain a hearing before the Executive Ethics Commission, and a circuit judge ruled he was entitled to one.
ethics.outcome: In January 2025 the Executive Ethics Commission ruled that the inspector general failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Tracy violated the law. Cleared.

record.title: Housing PLUS Act of 2025 (H.R. 5618)
record.detail: Reintroduced a bill directing HUD to give at least 50% of Continuum of Care homelessness funding to providers that offer wraparound services such as job training and addiction treatment, moving away from the "Housing First" approach. record.title: End Government Shutdowns Act (H.R. 5542)
record.detail: Introduced a bill to start automatic continuing appropriations whenever regular spending bills lapse: 99% of the prior year's level for 30 days, then 1% less every 30 days until a budget passes. It was referred to the House Appropriations Committee with no further action.

record.title: FIRM Act (H.R. 2702)
record.detail: Introduced, with Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY), a bill barring federal banking regulators from using "reputational risk" in supervising banks. record.title: Rectifying UDAAP Act (H.R. 1652)

ethics.title: Perjury and false-statement charges (Hubbard grand jury)
ethics.summary: While a state representative, Moore was arrested in April 2014 and charged with two counts of perjury and two counts of making false statements over his January 2014 testimony to the Lee County grand jury investigating then-House Speaker Mike Hubbard. Prosecutors alleged he testified falsely about when he learned an economic-development project in Enterprise was in jeopardy; they presented recorded conversations between Moore and his primary opponent Josh Pipkin.
ethics.outcome: Acquitted: a jury found him not guilty on all charges on October 30, 2014.

record.title: Declined to withdraw in favor of Bodnar
record.detail: Stayed in the race on the last day a candidate could withdraw from the general-election ballot. The party briefly posted, in error, that she had suspended her campaign.

ethics.title: Sex-discrimination lawsuit against the University of Montana
ethics.summary: In August 2021, 18 current and former employees sued UM alleging sex discrimination, saying the university was a "good ol' boys club" and that Bodnar perpetuated a culture that created wage, promotion and opportunity gaps for women. UM did not admit wrongdoing; a spokesman said the university was confident it would have won at trial.
ethics.outcome: Settled in January 2024 for $350,000 with commitments to Title IX training and a one-year independent Title IX review; dismissed with prejudice.

ethics.title: Complaints over petition signature gathering

Separately, Cascade County authorities are investigating about 800 possibly bogus signatures collected by at least one petitioner working for Bodnar and House independent Michael Eisenhauer.
ethics.outcome: No violation determination reported; investigators said none of the disputed Cascade County signatures counted toward qualification, both campaigns cooperated and neither campaign is suspected of wrongdoing (investigation ongoing as of Sept. 10, 2026).
